common_name: Rotundifolia Boxwood (Large Round-Leaf Vigorous English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotundifolia is a large, vigorous, round-leaved English boxwood selection suited to tall hedges and screens rather than small formal edging.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its eventual large size can be accommodated. Rotundifolia is among the most vigorous and cold-hardy of the English boxwood cultivars, bearing broad, rounded, glossy dark-green leaves noticeably larger than those of dwarf boxwood selections, and it takes on a bronze-purple cast in winter cold. Its upright, dense growth habit makes it a favored choice for tall screening hedges and large specimen shrubs rather than clipped low borders. It tolerates poorly drained sites somewhat better than many boxwoods but still performs best with sharp drainage to avoid root rot.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in evenly moist, well-drained loam in full sun to partial shade, choosing a site sheltered from harsh winter wind at the cold edge of its range; Harland boxwood is a heat- and humidity-tolerant species from China valued in the Southeast.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained loam, clay, or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. Harland boxwood forms a small, bushy, multi-stemmed mound of glossy bright-green leaves, each notched at the tip, and bears fragrant pale-yellow flowers in spring along attractive whitish stems. It tolerates summer heat and humidity notably better than English or littleleaf boxwood and shows good resistance to several soilborne diseases that trouble other Buxus species, though its cold hardiness is more limited and it needs wind protection at the northern edge of its range. Plants sold as Harland boxwood in southern nurseries are sometimes actually the similar Buxus bodinieri, so source from a supplier who verifies identification.

common_name: Curly Locks Boxwood (Twisted-Branch Curled-Leaf Dwarf Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Curly Locks is a novelty littleleaf boxwood selection grown for its twisted branches and curled foliage rather than for formal shearing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, protected from harsh winter wind. Curly Locks develops distinctively twisted, contorted branches bearing narrow, curled yellow-green leaves, giving it a shaggy, textural appearance unlike any clipped boxwood form, with insignificant but fragrant pale-yellow spring flowers. Its irregular mounding habit makes it a conversation-piece specimen or container subject in a shaded border rather than a hedge plant, and it is best left unsheared so the curling branch structure remains visible. Like other boxwoods it needs sharp drainage to avoid root rot and benefits from monitoring for boxwood leafminer and mites.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Glencoe (sold as Chicagoland Green) was selected by the Chicago Botanic Garden and Morton Arboretum for reliable survival in harsh northern winters.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, though growth is fullest and densest in full sun. Glencoe forms a uniform, broad, mounded shrub of soft green foliage closely resembling English boxwood in appearance, but it was bred and trialed specifically for extreme cold tolerance, reportedly showing no dieback at temperatures near thirty degrees below zero. Foliage bronzes only slightly in winter and greens back up quickly as temperatures rise in spring. Its reliable hardiness makes it a go-to boxwood for formal hedging in the Upper Midwest and other regions where standard English boxwood cultivars struggle to survive winter.
